activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, a team scores a goal by getting the ball into the other team's net.
story:
Maeve went to the big field with Mama and Pop. There were many people there. They all sat on a blanket in the grass. Maeve could see two nets, one at each end.

A big game started. People ran and kicked a ball. Maeve watched the ball go up high. She thought the ball had to go over the net. "Up, up!" she said. She pointed at the sky.

Then a player kicked the ball low. It rolled on the grass. It went right into the net. The net moved and the ball stayed inside. Everyone clapped and cheered. Maeve jumped up. Her tummy felt funny and happy.

Later, Maeve skipped over to a small ball by the fence. She kicked it toward a cone. The ball rolled in behind the cone and stopped. "It went in!" said Maeve. Mama laughed and clapped too. "Again," said Maeve, and she ran to get her ball.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: Ten is written with two digits, a 1 and then a 0.
story:
Madelyn went to the library in the morning. She wanted to make her very own counting book. One kitten, two shoes, three red apples, and more, all the way to ten.

She drew and drew. Then she got to the ten page. Ten needed a number, but Madelyn felt stuck. All the other numbers had one shape. She wrote a big 1. It did not look right all alone. Her tummy felt funny.

The librarian came close. "Can I help?" she asked. Madelyn showed her page. The librarian smiled and wrote on her own paper. Madelyn watched. First a 1, then a 0, side by side. Madelyn tried it. A 1 and then a 0. Ten! It looked just right.

Madelyn read her book out loud. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The librarian clapped. Madelyn hugged her book. "Can we take it home?" she asked. "Yes," said Mommy. Madelyn smiled and held it tight.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Charlotte went to the store with Mama. She held the shopping bag with both hands. Charlotte wanted a new crayon. She wanted to draw the sky.

First she found the crayon bin. She saw a red crayon. Red like a big apple. She saw a yellow crayon. Yellow like the sun. She saw a green crayon. Green like the grass. Then she found a gray crayon. "This one is for the sky," Charlotte said.

Mama needed a hot pizza for dinner. The store lady used big gloves. She put the hot pizza in a box. Mama carried the box, because it was hot. Charlotte did not touch it.

Charlotte held her gray crayon. Then she looked out the big window. The sun was out. It was a clear, sunny day. The sky was not gray. The sky was blue! Charlotte put the gray crayon back. She took a blue crayon instead.

At home, Charlotte sat at the little table. Mama opened the pizza box. The pizza was still hot, so Mama cut it into small pieces. Charlotte waited, then took a bite. Then she tried to draw her picture. Blue went on top, all across the sky. Green went on the bottom, for the grass. Yellow went in the corner, for the sun.

"Look, Mama," said Charlotte. "Blue sky, sunny day."

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
story:
Michael ran to the cookie jar. Grandma had just put out warm cookies. Michael reached out his hand. Then he stopped.

He looked down at his fingers. They had dirt on them. He had planted seeds in the garden that morning.

Michael ran to the sink. He pushed the soap pump. The soap felt smooth and slippery. He rubbed his hands together. He counted slowly to twenty. "One, two, three," he said. Bubbles grew big and white. They smelled like lemons.

He rinsed the bubbles away. He dried his hands on the soft towel. Then he ran back to Grandma. He picked up a cookie and took a big bite.

Grandma smiled and gave him a second cookie. "Crunchy one for you," she said.

Michael looked at his clean pink fingers. He took another happy bite.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: When someone says 'thank you', people often answer 'you're welcome.'
story:
Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a little bag of crackers. "Crackers, please," said her brother, Ben. Sadie did not know what to say. Then she said, "Yes, please wait." She gave Ben a cracker, slowly, one at a time.

Ben ate the cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," he said. Sadie was quiet. What could she say back? She looked out the window. She saw a cow by a fence. She heard the cow go moo. Then she heard Mom say, "You're welcome, Ben." Mom had given Ben a puzzle book. Ben had said thank you to Mom first.

Sadie saw it. Someone says thank you. Then someone says you're welcome. The words went back and forth, like a ball. Ben held out his hand. "Another cracker, please?" he asked. Sadie gave him one. "Thank you, Sadie," said Ben. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Mom smiled in the mirror. "Cool words," said Sadie, and she read the cover of Ben's puzzle book all the way home.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Two groups have the same number when each object in one group can be matched with one object in the other.
story:
Snack time was coming. Ruby wanted to set the big table. Her teacher, Miss Ana, gave her a basket of cups.

"Count them," said Miss Ana. Ruby touched each cup. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight cups. Then she counted the chairs. Eight chairs.

"Which has more?" Miss Ana asked. Ruby looked and looked. The cups were in a jumble. The chairs were in a row. She could not tell. "I don't know," she said. "How can I find out?"

Then Ruby had an idea. She put one cup in front of one chair. One cup, one chair. She went all the way around the table. One cup, one chair. One cup, one chair. Her friend Ben watched and handed her a shiny spoon for each cup, too.

At the last chair, Ruby put down the last cup. Her basket was empty. Every chair had a cup. Every cup had a chair. Nothing was left over. "They match!" said Ruby. "Same number!"

Ben picked up his cup and took a big drink of water. "Good counting, Ruby," he said. Ruby lifted her cup, and it went click against Ben's, like a little cheer.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Taking photos on a trip lets a family remember it after they get home.
story:
Lea packed her little red bag. "We are going to the beach!" she sang. The car ride was long. Lea counted three cows, then five cows, then she fell asleep.

At the beach, the water went splash, splash, splash. Lea found a shell with a hole in it. "Dad, take my picture!" she said. Dad held the camera. Click! "Now hold the shell up," said Dad. Click! Click!

Mom took a photo of the sand castle. Lea put seaweed on top. "It has hair!" she laughed. Mom laughed too. Click!

Then it was time to go home. The beach was far away now. Lea missed the waves. She missed the splash, splash, splash.

"Look," said Mom. She opened the photos on the big chair. There was Lea with her shell! There was the castle with seaweed hair! There was Dad with sand on his nose.

"Grandpa wants to see the beach too," said Dad.

"Then he can look at my pictures!" said Lea. "Click!"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together.
story:
Athena went to Miss Kim's music room. Big drums sat in a circle. Athena picked a small red drum. Her friend Leo picked a blue one.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy. Big gray clouds moved by.

"Now we play together," said Miss Kim. Athena tapped fast. Leo tapped fast too. Their drums went boom-boom-boom. It was too fast. They bumped sticks and stopped.

"Why did we stop?" asked Athena.

"We did not go the same speed," said Leo.

Miss Kim clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. It was slow and even. Athena clapped too. Leo clapped too. Then they tapped their drums just like the claps. Tap, tap, tap. Slow and even. The two drums sounded like one big drum.

Then came the surprise. Athena tapped her drum, and Leo's drum made the same sound back. "It is like a picture in a mirror!" Athena said.

"Thank you, Miss Kim," Athena said. She tapped some more, slow and even, all the way to the end.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A vegetable plant that does not get enough water droops.
story:
Nolan ran to the garden with his small red watering can. "Can I plant lettuce today?" he asked. His grandma smiled. "Yes, we can plant it together." They patted the smooth brown dirt. Nolan dropped tiny seeds into the hole. He covered them up, pat, pat, pat. Then he gave them a drink of water.

Every day Nolan came back. The sun was hot. The lettuce grew small and green. But one morning the leaves were drooping. They hung down low. "Are you sleepy?" Nolan asked. He touched a leaf. It felt soft and sad. "Maybe you need water!" he said.

Nolan filled his can at the pond nearby. He poured water all over the leaves. Drip, drip, drip. The next day the lettuce stood up tall. "Look, Grandma!" Nolan shouted. "It's not droopy anymore!" Grandma clapped her hands. Nolan watered the plants every single day after that.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cake batter is runny when it goes into the oven and comes out as a cake you can slice.
story:
Theodore went to the farmers' market with Dad. He held the basket with both hands. They needed eggs, milk and butter. Theodore picked the eggs one by one. He did not let them knock together. "Good job," said Dad.

At home, Theodore had big news. "I will bake Papa's birthday cake!" he said. Dad helped him crack the eggs. Theodore poured in the milk. He stirred and stirred. The batter was thin and runny. It went slosh in the bowl.

Theodore looked worried. "This is not a cake," he said. "It is just wet soup. Papa will have birthday soup." He stuck his finger in the bowl. The batter dripped off, drip drip drip. "A cake is big and round. This is not round at all!"

Dad poured the batter into a pan. He put the pan in the hot oven. Theodore watched from his stool, far away. The kitchen began to smell sweet. Theodore waited and waited.

Then Dad opened the oven. Out came a real cake! It was big and golden. Dad turned it out of the pan. Then he cut it, and each slice came out soft and neat. "Papa gets a lion on top," said Theodore. "With a frozen strawberry for its nose!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow melts into water when it is brought inside where it is warm.
story:
Lucy woke up and saw white outside. No school today! It was a snow day. She put on her red hat and her warm boots. Then she ran to the sledding hill with Dad.

Lucy went down the hill on her sled. Whee! She rolled off into the soft snow. A little leaf was stuck to her mitten. That was funny. Lucy wanted to keep some snow too. She made a small snowball. She put it in her pocket and zipped it up tight, like a lock.

At home, Lucy reached into her pocket. She felt something wet. The snowball was gone! There was just a puddle in her pocket. Lucy held up her wet mitten. "Dad, look! My snow turned into water!" Dad helped her hang the wet mitten by the fire. Lucy laughed and patted her pocket dry.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: People often write their name on their artwork so everyone knows who made it.
story:
Maverick sat at the little red table. He had one sheet of paper. He had one fat crayon. He drew a cat with a long tail. One cat, one tail, one happy smile.

Next to him, his friend Nina drew too. She made a cat as well. Her cat had a long tail too. Then the teacher said, "Put your papers on the big shelf." Maverick put his paper down. Nina put her paper down. Then two papers sat side by side. They looked the same.

"Which one is mine?" Maverick asked. He looked and looked. He could not tell. Nina could not tell either. Her lip began to wobble. Maverick wanted to help her. He was kind to his friend.

Then he had an idea. "I can write my name," he said. He picked up the crayon. M for Maverick. A for Maverick. He wrote it on his cat. "This one is mine!" The other one had to be Nina's. Nina hugged her paper. "Thank you, Maverick," she said.

"Now we both know," said Nina. She wrote her name too. One name, two names, two cats, two smiles. Maverick tapped his paper. "Hello, Maverick's cat," he said.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Looking at the target while you throw helps you aim.
story:
Brielle ran into the sunny backyard. Daddy held up a big red hoop. "Throw the beanbag in!" he said.

Brielle had a yellow beanbag. She squeezed it. Then she saw her friend Milo at the fence. "Hi, Milo!" she called. She waved and threw the beanbag. It landed in the grass. It missed the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle.

Daddy held the hoop up again. "One, two, three, throw!" This time Brielle looked at the hoop. She looked and looked. Then she let the beanbag go. It flew through the hoop. It hit the ground with a little sound, pat!

"I did it!" said Brielle. She jumped up and down. "Again! Again!" Daddy tossed her a big blue ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. The wind began to blow. The ball wobbled in the air. Brielle held out both hands. She held on tight. She caught it!

Milo clapped at the fence. Brielle held the ball up high. "Look, Milo, I caught it!" she said.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a sunny day, a sun hat helps shade your face.
story:
Claire stood at the front door. She wanted to play outside. But which clothes should she wear?

She looked out the window. The wind blew the big tree. Leaves flew all around. "It is windy today," said Mom. "Wear your jacket." Claire put on her jacket. The jacket flapped like a flag.

Then the sky grew dark. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Puddles formed on the path. "It is rainy now," said Mom. "Where are your boots?" Claire found her yellow boots. She stepped in a puddle. Splash! She sailed a leaf like a little boat on the water.

Next the rain turned to snow. White flakes fell on the grass. The snow did not melt. It stayed on the ground. "Snowy days need mittens," said Mom. Claire pulled on her red mittens.

At last the sun came out. It was sunny and bright. Claire ran to the swing. The sun shone in her eyes. She squinted and squeezed her eyes shut. She could not see her swing at all.

Mom came out with a hat. "Try this, Claire." Claire put on the sun hat. The hat shaded her face. Now she could open her eyes wide. She swung high and laughed.

"Best hat ever!" she said.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: If two children want the same toy, a grown-up can help them take turns.
story:
Layla ran to the toy corner fast. A little blue truck sat on the rug. She wanted it so much.

Ben grabbed the truck too. They pulled. The truck went back and forth. It nearly fell.

Layla let go. She looked at Teacher May. "We both need the truck," she said.

Teacher May smiled. "Let's take turns," she said. "Ben first. Then Layla."

Layla sat on the rug. She watched Ben drive the truck. It went zoom, zoom, zoom.

Then Teacher May said, "Layla's turn." Ben gave her the truck. Layla drove it to the block tower.

"My turn," said Ben. Layla gave the truck back. He drove it under the table.

Layla waited again. She clapped when Ben zoomed by. Soon it was her turn once more.

"Your turn is fast," said Layla. She pushed the truck all the way to the door. Ben laughed and held out his hands.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Small toys can roll or slide under furniture like couches and beds.
story:
Ibrahim went to the park with Mama. He brought his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. The grass was wet from last night's rain. The air smelled like winter was coming.

Ibrahim set his car on the bench. Then he ran to pet a small brown dog. When he came back, the car was gone. He looked at the bench seat. He looked at the ground by his shoes. No car anywhere.

"I will try one more spot," he said. He got down on his knees. He peeked under the bench. The blue car sat there in the shade. It had rolled off the seat and slid underneath. A tiny ladybug sat on top of it.

Ibrahim reached in and pulled the car out. The ladybug flew away on red wings. "Hello again," Ibrahim said to his car. He held it tight in both hands all the way home.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Many drawing apps let you pick a colour by tapping it.
story:
Leah sat on the big rug in the living room. She wanted to draw a red sun. "Where is the red?" she asked. Mom helped her hold the tablet and press the little button. The screen lit up. Leah tapped the drawing app with one finger. It opened!

At the bottom of the screen there were small round colours. Leah tapped the blue one. Her finger made a blue line. Then she tapped the red one. Her finger made a red line. "I tapped red, and now I draw red!" she said. She drew a big red sun with soft yellow rays. "Is the sun too hot?" she asked herself. "No, it is a paper sun. It cannot be hot at all."

Leah drew a green hill under the sun. She drew a small brown dog on the hill. When she was done, she looked at her picture. "All finished," she said. Mom showed her how to press the button once more. The screen went dark and quiet. "I will put it away now," Leah said. She carried the tablet with two hands. She set it in its safe spot on the shelf. Then she ran to tell Mom, "I turned it on, I drew a sun, and I put it away all by myself!"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
story:
Theo went to the community center with his dad. There was a music room with small chairs. On a table lay some recorders.

Theo picked up a blue recorder. He wanted to play his favorite song, the duck song. He blew into the recorder. It made a loud squeak. Theo tried again. Squeak, squeak.

A girl named Maya sat next to him. She put her fingers flat on the holes. Then she blew. A nice low note came out. Theo looked at her fingers.

Theo pressed his finger on one hole. He blew. The sound was low. He lifted his finger off the hole. He blew again. The sound was high. Theo tried another hole. He got a new note.

Soon Theo played a tune. Maya clapped. Theo played some more. "Quack, quack," he sang, and the recorder went low, low.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, lion dancers move to the beat of loud drums.
story: Isabelle held Mama's hand at the cultural center. It was a big Lunar New Year party. There were red lanterns and paper flowers everywhere. Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! Boom! Isabelle covered her ears. "Too loud!" she said. She hid behind Mama's coat. "Will the loud noise hurt me?" she asked. "No," said Mama. "Just listen. Watch the lion." Isabelle peeked out. The big lion dance was starting. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion shook its head. Isabelle watched and watched. "The lion jumps when the drum goes boom!" she said. Mama smiled and nodded. Isabelle let go of her ears. She clapped along with the drums. The lion jumped and spun. Isabelle laughed and clapped louder. "It is not a rainy day," said Mama, "so we can stay outside as long as we like." After the party, Mama said, "Then we will go home, and I will bathe you in warm, soapy water." Isabelle clapped her hands one more time. "Boom!" she said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: A kitchen timer beeps or rings to tell the cook it is time to check the food.
story:
David stood at the big table in the cooking classroom. He was making muffins for his family. He stirred the batter round and round. His teacher, Miss Ana, put the pan in the oven. She turned a little knob. "Now we set the timer," she said.

The timer ticked and ticked. David drew a fox on paper while he waited. Then he and his dad began to play a game with red cards. David got busy matching the cards. He forgot all about the muffins.

Beep! Beep! The timer rang out loud. David jumped up. "The muffins!" he said. Miss Ana put on big mitts and took out the pan. The muffins were round and golden. "Smell them," said Dad. David sniffed. They smelled sweet. "The timer told us," said David, and he clapped his hands.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: It is okay for a big brother or sister to feel left out when a new baby arrives.
story:
Florence sat in a big chair by the window. Mom held a tiny baby in her arms. "This is your new sister," Mom said. Florence looked and looked. The baby was small like a little mouse. Florence wanted to hold her. "Not yet," said Dad. "She is too tiny." Florence's face felt hot. "No fair," she said. "Everyone looks at the baby. No one looks at me." She hid behind the curtain. The curtain was soft and cool.

Mom called, "Florence, come here." Florence came slowly. Mom patted the chair. "Sit close to me." Florence sat. Mom gave her a kiss. "You can miss me. That is okay. I still love you big." Dad got paper. Florence began to draw. She drew the baby. She drew Mom. She drew herself. The wrong color went on the baby's face. Florence laughed. "She is green!" Mom laughed too. Florence drew one more picture. "This one is for the baby," she said.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
story: Ali ran into the big kitchen. "I want to help!" he said. Miss Rosa smiled. "Wash your hands," she said. "Then you can make toast." Ali washed his hands. The toast was ready. Miss Rosa had made it on the hot stove. Now it sat on the cool table. Ali held the butter knife. He spread the butter. Slow, slow, slow. The butter went soft and smooth. "Look at my toast!" he said. "So smooth!" "Very nice," said Miss Rosa. "You are a cute little helper. Now pour some milk." Ali got the little jug of milk. He poured and poured. The cup filled up to the very top. Ali picked up the cup. He took one step. Milk spilled over the edge. It ran down his hand and onto the floor. Ali got a cloth. He wiped the spill. Then he poured again. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. Ali picked up the cup. He walked across the kitchen. Not one drop spilled! Outside the window, snow was starting to fall. "Look, Ali!" said Miss Rosa. Ali sat down with his toast and his milk. He took a big bite and a big sip. "Mmm," he said. "I did it all by myself."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book.
story:
Eva went to the library with Mama. She found a book with a bear on the front. The bear wore a red hat. Eva loved the pictures. "Who drew this bear?" she asked.

Mama said, "Let's look inside." Eva grabbed the book. She opened the front cover first. There was a page with names on it. Mama pointed to one name. "That name is the artist," Mama said. "An illustrator made these pictures." Eva put her finger on the name. "The illustrator made my bear," she said.

Eva turned the pages one by one. The story went from the first page to the last page. The bear found his red hat at the very end. "Again!" said Eva. Mama laughed and turned back to the front. Eva hugged the book tight and whispered, "Hello, bear."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: In pretend play, a cardboard box can become a car, a boat or a house.
story:
Leah saw a big cardboard box at school. She wanted it to be a house. She put her teddy bear inside. "This is teddy's house," she said.

Then Ben came. He wanted the box too. "It's a car," said Ben. "Beep beep!" Leah held the box hard. Ben pulled the other side. Teddy fell out. His hat fell in the bucket of toys.

Miss Rosa came over. "You can take turns," she said. Ben went first. He drove the box car around the rug. Leah waited. She picked up teddy and his hat.

Then it was Leah's turn. The same box became a house again! She tucked teddy in with a small blanket. Ben knocked on the wall. "May teddy come out to play?" he asked. Leah smiled. "Yes! Bring your car. Teddy needs a ride."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food.
story:
Everly was at Grandma's house. Baby Jack was sleeping in a soft basket. Everly wanted to give him a present.

She found a cracker in her pocket. It was a good cracker. She held it out to the baby. "Jack, look! A cracker for you!"

Jack woke up. He opened his tiny mouth. He made a little cry. Everly put the cracker close, but Grandma came over fast. "Babies can't eat crackers yet," Grandma said. "Baby Jack only drinks milk."

Everly looked at the cracker. Then she looked at Jack. He was still crying. His tummy was rumbling loud.

Everly followed Grandma to the table. Grandma picked up a small bottle. The milk inside was warm, not hot. Grandma held the bottle, and Jack grabbed it with both tiny hands. He drank and drank. His eyes got sleepy and cool and calm. The crying stopped.

"More milk?" Everly asked.

"Maybe later," Grandma said.

Everly sat down beside the basket. She ate her cracker, bite by bite. Jack watched her with big eyes. "When you are big," Everly said, "I will give you one."

Jack made a small milk smile.

"Shh," said Everly. "Sleep now, Jack."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
story:
Nova was at daycare. It was show and tell day. She had a small toy tooth from her dentist kit. She wanted to show it to everyone. But her tummy felt jumpy. She felt afraid to talk in front of the class. Her hands hid the tooth behind her back.

Then Nova saw her teacher, Miss Kim. Miss Kim's hands were shaking too. "I always feel nervous on show and tell day," Miss Kim said. Nova looked up. Grown-ups feel like this too? That made her feel less alone. Miss Kim took a big breath. So Nova took a big breath too. Miss Kim smiled. Nova smiled.

Nova walked to the front. She held up the tooth. "This is a tooth," she said. Her voice was small but it stayed strong. The class clapped. Nova felt a big, warm, happy feeling. Miss Kim clapped loudest of all.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Starting a question with 'May I' is a polite way to ask permission.
story:
Mason wanted his toy lion. It was up on a big shelf. He reached and reached. His fingers could not touch it.

He tried to shake the shelf a little. The lion did not move. Mom came into the room. "Mason, what do you need?" she asked.

Mason said, "Help, please." Mom smiled. "May I have the lion?" Mason asked. Mom said, "Yes, you may." She took the lion down and put it in his hands.

"Thank you," said Mason. He hugged the lion tight. Then his sister Mia walked in. She looked at the lion. She wanted a turn too.

"May I have a turn?" Mia asked. Mason thought for a minute. Then he said, "Yes, you may." Mia held the lion gently. She made it roar, "Roar!" Mason laughed.

Later Mason bumped into Mia's tower of blocks. The blocks fell down. "Sorry," said Mason. Mia patted his arm. "It is okay," she said. They built the tower again, tall and strong.

Mom brought two cups of milk. "Thank you," said Mason and Mia together. Mom sat on the couch with them. The lion sat on Mason's lap, all warm and safe.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
story:
Weston ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. He wanted to be a firefighter today. But the dress-up box looked all mixed up. There was a truck on top. There was a banana toy under a hat. His friend Pip had already taken the red firefighter coat.

Weston found one red sock. He put the sock in the toy bin. Then he laughed. A sock was not a toy. A sock was a hat for your foot. He moved the sock to the pile of shirts and hats. Shirts, socks and hats all went together. Now the pile looked neat.

Miss Joy came over to help. "You made a sorting place," she said. Weston put the truck with the toys. He put the play bananas and apples with the foods. The dress-up box was easy to open now. Pip hung the red coat on a hook, but the hat shelf was empty.

Weston looked and looked. Where was a firefighter hat? He felt worried. Then he saw something sticky on the shape table. It was a triangle hat made of paper! Miss Joy had made it just for him. Weston put it on his head. "I am the firefighter!" he said. Pip handed him a toy hose.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
story:
Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad held her hand. They walked to the playground.

Violet wanted to go on the swing. But a big kid was on it. "Can I have a turn, please?" asked Violet. The big kid slid down. "Thank you!" said Violet. She pumped her legs. The swing went high.

Then a boy came by. He had a truck. He hid behind his dad. He peeked out at Violet. Violet smiled. "Hello!" she said. The boy peeked out more. "Hello," he said back, very small. Then he rolled his truck to her feet.

"I can push it to you," said Violet. She pushed too hard. The truck bumped his toe. "Sorry," said Violet. "It's okay," said the boy.

Dad called, "Snack time!" Violet held the boy's hand. They ran to the bench together.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A map shows roads and places, so people can find the way somewhere new.
story:
Sienna sat on the train with Mama and Papa. She was going on a family trip, far from home. "One bag, one bear, one hat," she counted. "One little Sienna!" said Papa with a smile.

After the train, they got in the car. Papa drove and drove. "Oh dear," said Papa. "I do not know this road." He stopped the car. The windows were down, and the air smelled fresh like grass.

Sienna looked at her book. It was not a storybook. It had lines and little pictures. Roads and towns and rivers. It was a map. She put her finger on a line. "Our train went here," she said. Then she slid her finger along. "And the road goes this way!"

Papa leaned over and looked. "You found it, Sienna!" He drove where her finger pointed. One bend, two bends, three. Then a small white house appeared. A cow stood by the fence. It mooed at them.

Grandma opened the door. "My sweet friend!" she said, hugging Sienna. Inside, there was ice cream in little bowls. Sienna ate hers slowly and watched it melt. "The map got us here," she whispered to her bear. "All the way here."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
story:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. He wanted his favorite book. But which one was it? Grandma had so many books on the shelf.

"Can you find the one that is yours?" Grandma asked. Aaron looked and looked. Then he saw something. His school bag sat by the door. It had a little card on it. The card said AARON. Grandma handed him a birthday card. It said AARON too.

"Look, Grandma, it is the same!" Aaron said. The letters were the same. The letters were in the same order. He traced them with his finger. A, A, R, O, N. Then he traced them again on his bag. A, A, R, O, N.

"Now hurry," said Grandma. "Find a book with your name." Aaron picked up a big book. He opened the front cover. There it was. AARON, written right inside. "This one is mine!" he said. "It is my favorite book!"

He sat on Grandma's soft lap. Grandma turned the pages one by one, front to back. "My name, then the story," Aaron said. He snuggled close. Grandma read to him until bedtime.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: The dentist's chair tips back so you lie down while the dentist looks in your mouth.
story:
Willow sat in the car with her teddy bear. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "Open wide," she said to teddy. Teddy did not open. "You try it," said Mom. Willow opened her own mouth wide. "Very good," said Mom.

At the dentist's office there was a big chair. Willow was scared of the big chair. She held her teddy tight. "You can sit on my lap," said Mom. So Willow sat with Mom, and the chair went up with them too.

Then the chair began to tip back. It leaned and leaned, like a slow ride. Willow giggled. She was lying down, and teddy sat on her tummy. "I fall back like a leaf," she laughed. The dentist looked in her mouth. "Smart girl," said the dentist. "Open wide." And Willow opened wide, just like she had practiced.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green.
story:
Joshua sat at the picnic table. Summer camp was loud today. Birds sang high in the trees. His sun hat sat next to his paper. He was painting a big park.

He painted a slide. He painted a blue sky. Then he wanted grass. He looked in his paint box. There was no green paint. He looked again. Only blue and yellow.

"I need green," he said. His friend Mia looked over. "Try mixing two colors," she said. Joshua put blue on his brush. He put yellow on top. He swirled them on the paper. The paint turned green!

Joshua clapped his hands. He painted green grass all along the bottom. He painted a green tree too. The teacher hung his picture on the fence. "Look at my park!" said Joshua.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Toys cannot really feel, but you can pretend they do.
story:
Gabriella went to Mia's house to play. Mia had a big spotted doll named Bob. Bob had a cloth swimming pool on the floor.

Mia dropped Bob on the rug. Mia began to cry. "Bob fell! He is sad!"

Mia's mom came over. She picked up Bob. "Bob is fine," she said. "Dolls cannot really feel. But you can pretend he does."

Mia stopped crying. She gave Bob a hug. Then she kissed his soft spotted head.

Gabriella watched. Then she held up a toy duck. "My duck fell too," she said. She dropped the duck on purpose. Then she picked it up and hugged it. "All better, little duck."

The girls put bandages on all the toys. Bob got the biggest bandage. Then they laid the toys on a towel. "The toys swam all day," said Gabriella. "Now they need a nap."

Mia covered Bob with a small blanket. "Shh," she said. "Bob is sleeping."

Gabriella put her finger to her lips. "He is a sleepy spotted swimmer," she whispered.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Words are all around us, on signs, labels and boxes, and they tell us things.
story:
Asher went to the store with Mama. He wanted apple juice. "Find the juice, Asher," said Mama. Asher looked and looked. The boxes were tall, tall, tall. He could not find any juice.

Then Asher saw little marks on a box. "Mama, what are these?" he asked. "Those are words," said Mama. "Words hide on boxes and tell us things." Asher looked at another box. "Words!" he said. Another box. "More words!" He counted them out loud. "One box, two boxes, three boxes, all full of words."

Mama pointed to a red box. "These words say apple juice." Asher hugged the box. It was soft and squishy on top. He carried it to the cart. At home, Mama opened a book. She read from the front page first. Asher turned the pages, one by one, all by himself. "Again!" he said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Hosts show a guest where things are, like the towels and the bathroom.
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor skipped around the backyard with him. They looked at the tiny ants on the step. "Where do they go?" she wondered.

On the second night, Grandpa took a bath. Then he called out, "Where are the towels?" Eleanor ran down the hall. She opened the tall cupboard. The towels were stacked in the middle, right where Mom always put them. She pulled one out and gave it to Grandpa. "Here you go!" she said.

The next morning, Grandpa wanted to wash his hands. "Where is the bathroom?" he asked. Eleanor laughed. She took his big hand and led him down the hall. "This door," she said. Grandpa smiled and patted his hands dry. Eleanor puffed up her chest like a proud little host. "I know where everything is," she whispered.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Cooper ran to the art room. He loved paint day. He sat down at the big table. His friend Mia put on her apron. Cooper did not put one on. He wanted to start right away.

Cooper dipped his brush in blue paint. He made a big swoosh. A dot of paint fell on his shirt. It was his favorite shirt. Another dot fell. Oh no. Blue spots everywhere.

The teacher brought Cooper an old shirt. "Put this on," she said. Cooper put it over his favorite shirt. Then he painted a happy dog. Paint splashed on the old shirt. He looked down. His favorite shirt was still clean under it.

At the sink, Cooper washed his hands in the glass window's bright light. The room was noisy with happy painters. "Next time, apron first," Cooper said to Mia. He smiled and held up his painting for his mom.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Lining two groups up side by side, one across from one, shows which has more: the group with some left over.
story:
Raphael ran to the block corner at the community centre. The sun came in through the big window. His friend Mia was there too. They both grabbed blocks.

"I have more," said Mia. "No, I have more," said Raphael. He asked himself, how can we know? He looked at his blocks. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Mia counted hers. "One, two, three, four, five, six." But which pile was more? The piles looked the same.

Raphael had an idea. "Let's line them up," he said. He put his blocks in a row. Mia put hers in a row right across from his. One block faced one block. Then another faced another. At the end, Raphael had one block with no friend facing it. "My row is longer," said Raphael. "So I have one more."

Mia's lip began to melt into a sad face. Raphael counted his blocks again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He picked up the last block, the one with no friend. "Here," he said. "Now we both have six." Then they built one big tower together. But it wobbled, and it fell. The tower was broken! They laughed and counted the fallen blocks all over again.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Small children sometimes sit on a booster seat so the hairdresser can reach their hair.
story:
Nolan went to Grandpa's house for a fun day. "We are going somewhere special," said Grandpa. "You get your first haircut!" Nolan patted his hair. "My hair is getting long," he said.

They walked to the salon. It was bright and shiny inside. There was a big chair that went up and down. Nolan jumped on. But he was too small. The hairdresser could not reach the top of his head. "Hmm," she said with a smile.

The hairdresser brought a booster seat. It was like the one at the playground, small and strong. She set it on the big chair. Nolan climbed up and sat on it. Now he was tall! "I can see the mirror," said Nolan. The hairdresser could reach all his hair now.

Snip, snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the clean white cape. Nolan watched each piece fall. He wiggled his toes. The booster seat held him just right.

Grandpa gave him a big thumbs up. Then the hairdresser brushed him off, and Nolan hopped down. "All done!" he said. "Look at my short, clean hair, Grandpa!" Grandpa laughed and took his hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A scoreboard shows how many points each team has.
story:
Eliana sat on the soft rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Mom and Aunt Jo sat on the couch. Everyone was cheering.

"Who is winning?" Eliana asked. She could not remember the score. She asked again. "Who has more points?"

"Look up high," said Grandpa. He pointed to the TV.

Eliana looked. There it was. A big bright board at the top of the screen. It had numbers on it. One side had a red four. The other side had a blue six.

"Blue is winning!" Eliana said. She clapped her hands.

The blue team ran fast. They kicked the ball. The net moved. The crowd on TV got loud. The big board changed to a blue seven.

"It went up!" Eliana said. She pulled her teddy bear close and hugged it.

Later the buzzer went off. The game was over. The curtains were closed and the room felt cozy. Grandpa picked Eliana up.

"Who won?" he asked her.

"Blue," said Eliana. "I looked at the board."
